opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a real gap there, and it's worth being honest about it.

Most of the models we've built so far, whether language models or image and video generation models, were trained on data from the digital world. Text on the internet, photos, videos people uploaded. They're very good at capturing what the world *looks like*, or what people *say* about the world. But a robot doesn't need to describe the world. It needs to act in it. And acting requires a different kind of understanding: geometry, physics, contact, cause and effect, what happens three seconds from now if I push this cup.

Take video generation as an example. A video model can produce a clip that looks completely plausible to a human viewer, but if you look closely, objects pass through each other, hands merge with what they're holding, mass and friction don't really behave consistently. For entertainment that's fine. Nobody minds. For a robot, that's exactly the information it can't do without. So the objective is different. In the digital world, the bar is perceptual realism. In the physical world, the bar is physical correctness and controllability.

There's also a mismatch in the form of the output. Digital-world models typically output pixels or tokens. A robot needs actions, and it needs them in closed loop, with low latency, responding to feedback. A model that takes several seconds to think before generating a beautiful answer isn't very useful when you're in the middle of grasping something that's slipping.

That said, I don't think the digital-world models are useless for robotics. Quite the opposite. They carry an enormous amount of prior knowledge: what objects are, how people usually use them, the semantics of a scene. That's very hard to get from robot data alone, because robot data is expensive and scarce. So I see the relationship as complementary. The digital-world models give you the common sense and the semantic understanding, and then you need something additional, whether that's 3D representations, world models that respect physics, simulation, or real interaction data, to ground that knowledge in the physical world.

This is a big part of why I've become so interested in world models. A good world model sits in between. It can learn from large-scale video, so it inherits the richness of digital data, but it's trained to predict how the world evolves in response to actions. Once you have that, it can serve as a simulator, as a data engine, and eventually as part of the robot's own brain for planning.

So my short answer is that the fit is partial. The digital-world models give us a strong starting point, but they're not the finish line. The hard and interesting work right now is figuring out how to bridge from "looks right" to "works right."

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the fit is partial, and the gap is more interesting than the overlap.

Large models trained on internet data have learned an enormous amount about what the world looks like and how people describe it. That transfers surprisingly well to robots at the level of understanding: recognizing objects, parsing an instruction like "put the cup on the shelf next to the kettle," reasoning about which steps come before which. A robot built five years ago had essentially no common sense. Today you can get a lot of it almost for free, and I don't want to understate how big a shift that is.

But the digital world has a property the physical world doesn't: the output is cheap and reversible. If a language model writes a wrong sentence, you regenerate. If an image model produces a wrong hand, nobody gets hurt. A robot acting in the world closes a loop. The action changes the state, the state changes what the robot sees, and a small error compounds within a few hundred milliseconds. Internet data tells you almost nothing about contact, friction, how an object deforms when you grip it, or what happens when your estimate of the table height is off by two centimeters. That knowledge lives in the interaction itself, not in text or video someone posted.

So the way I see it, pretrained models give robots the "semantic layer," and the hard open question is the layer underneath: perception that is grounded in geometry and physics, and control that can tolerate being wrong. The two layers also run at different speeds. A vision-language model thinking for a second is fine. A hand correcting its grip needs to react far faster than that. A lot of current system design is really about deciding where to draw the line between those two.

Where I'm most optimistic is video generation and world models. If a model can predict what the scene will look like after an action, you get something robots have always lacked: a way to imagine consequences before committing. That's closer to how the physical world actually works than any amount of text. But I'd caution against treating it as solved. Generating plausible video and generating physically correct video are not the same thing, and robots care about the second one.

So, a good fit for understanding and planning, a poor fit for the last ten centimeters. Most of the real work in the next few years, in my view, is in that last ten centimeters.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes semantic understanding from grounded perception and control, but does not propose aligning visual representations with robotic learning needs during encoder training.

r003.rationale: It says a vision-language model can take a second while a hand must react faster, but does not clearly state that digital-world generation applications tolerate more latency than physical-world robotics applications.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a strong connection, but also an important gap. In the digital world, a model mainly learns from representations of what has happened—text, images, videos. A robot has to take an action and deal with what happens next. It needs to understand not just what an object is, but whether it can grasp it, how much force to apply, and how that object will behave when it moves.

So digital models can provide a useful foundation, especially for recognizing things, understanding instructions, and bringing general knowledge into a task. But that doesn’t automatically translate into reliable physical behavior. A robot needs feedback from interaction: vision, touch, movement, and the consequences of its own actions.

The fit, to me, is complementary. We should build on what these models already know, while giving them a way to learn through action. The real test is whether a robot can notice that something isn’t going as expected and adjust, rather than simply execute a plan that sounded reasonable.

r003.rationale: The response makes no comparison between latency tolerated by digital generation and latency constraints in physical robotics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a gap between understanding the digital world and acting in the physical world. A model can describe what it sees, but a robot has to decide what to do, execute that action, and respond when the result is different from what it expected.

Digital models provide a useful foundation, especially for visual understanding, language, and general knowledge. But physical interaction adds things that are difficult to learn from images and text alone: force, friction, timing, and the consequences of an action. Recognizing a cup doesn’t necessarily mean knowing how tightly to grasp it.

So I see these models as a starting point. The challenge is connecting their knowledge to perception and control through experience in the physical world. That requires a loop: observe, act, get feedback, and adjust.
